title: The Estate, the Refinery, and the Garden Wall: Mosaddegh, the Oil, and the Coup
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Ahmadabad-e Mosaddeq, birth on the family estate
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: West of Tehran, in the flat country of Nazarabad under the Alborz, a son is born on the family estate to Mirza Hedayatollah, a treasury official of the Qajar administration, and to Malek Taj Khanom, who descends from the Qajar royal line. They name him Mohammad. The estate is called Ahmadabad; it will one day be called Ahmadabad-e Mosaddeq. He will spend the last eleven years of his life confined to this ground by a government, and he will be buried under the floor of its dining room.
suggested_refs: The Mosaddegh house at Ahmadabad-e Mosaddeq, Nazarabad County, Alborz Province

stops.name: Tehran, the house of a treasury official
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the father's death by cholera in 1892 is attested, but no address for the family house was located and the coordinates are an estimate for central old Tehran
stops.campa: Cholera takes Mirza Hedayatollah in 1892 and the boy passes into his mother's keeping. Najm al-Saltaneh raises him inside the bureaucratic caste she married into. Tutors come to the house to teach him French, arithmetic, and the etiquette of the treasury, where an office is inherited like a name. The counsel she gives him is not about advancement, and he repeats it for the rest of his life. In 1901 he marries Zahra Emami, called Khadijeh, herself of the Qajar line; she outlives the coup by twelve years and very nearly outlives him.
stops.quote: A person's worth in society is dependent on how much one endures for the sake of the people.
stops.quote_source: Najm al-Saltaneh, his mother, in words he recounted; rendered thus in tmj.news, 'The Overthrow of Mossadegh', and in The Friday Times, 'Remembering Mossadegh' (27 Feb 2015), which vary between 'the people' and 'his people' and which misattribute the line to Mosaddegh himself
suggested_refs: Najm al-Saltaneh, Mosaddegh's mother, and the counsel he attributed to her

stops.name: Isfahan, elected at twenty-four and refused the seat
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month attested and no specific Isfahan site is named in connection with the election
stops.campa: The Constitutional Revolution opens a parliament and Isfahan returns him to it. He is twenty-four. The electoral law of the new order sets thirty as the minimum age for a deputy, and the chamber he has been elected to will not seat him. He never sits in the first Majlis. The revolution that excludes him on a technicality is the one he spends the rest of his life defending as the only lawful source of Iranian government. He makes that argument against a shah in 1925, against a British company in 1951, and against an American agency in 1953.
suggested_refs: The electoral law of the first Majlis and its minimum age of thirty

stops.name: Paris, the Ecole libre des sciences politiques
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1909; the institution is named here as it stood in 1909, the Ecole libre des sciences politiques, not by its 1945 successor Sciences Po, which the first research pass anachronistically supplied
stops.campa: He goes to Paris to study political science at the Ecole libre des sciences politiques, the school that trains the administrators of the Third Republic. He belongs to a generation of Iranians sent west to learn the machinery of constitutional government and bring it home in working order. Illness ends the course after roughly two years and he takes no French degree. He returns to Iran to recover. Two years later he takes up the study again at Neuchatel, in Switzerland.
suggested_refs: The Ecole libre des sciences politiques, rue Saint-Guillaume, Paris, before its 1945 reconstitution

stops.name: Neuchatel, the doctorate in law
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1913; the claim that he was the first Iranian to hold a European law doctorate is hedged in the source itself as holding by most accounts
stops.campa: At the University of Neuchatel he completes the doctorate that France's climate denied him, writing on wills and testaments in Islamic law. By most accounts he is the first Iranian to hold a European doctorate in law. He goes home in 1914, into a country the Great War will occupy without asking permission, and takes up teaching at the Tehran School of Political Science, where the sons of the administrative class are trained. The law he is examined on in French is the law he argues against Britain forty years later.
suggested_refs: Mosaddegh's Neuchatel doctoral thesis on testamentary law in Islam
The Madrese-ye Olum-e Siyasi (Tehran School of Political Science), founded 1899

stops.name: Shiraz, governor-general of Fars
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1920-1921, correcting a first pass that anchored the provincial governorships at 1922; the month is not attested, and the Arg-e Karim Khan as his seat is an inference from the customary residence of Fars governors
stops.campa: He is made Minister of Justice in Tehran under Hassan Pirnia, and then, asked by petitioners while passing through the province, takes the governorship of Fars. He administers it from Shiraz, in the Zand citadel that has housed the region's rulers for a century and a half. His term is spent in dispute with the South Persia Rifles, a force raised, paid, and officered by the British inside Iranian territory. It is his first sustained quarrel with a foreign power operating a piece of his own country.
suggested_refs: The Arg-e Karim Khan, Shiraz, customary seat of the governors of Fars
The South Persia Rifles, British-officered, 1916-1921

stops.name: Tehran, the Ministry of Finance under Qavam
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 21 November 1921 to 7 January 1922; the ministry building coordinates are an estimate for central Tehran
stops.campa: Ahmad Qavam gives him the Ministry of Finance in November, in the unstable season between Reza Khan's coup of February and whatever Reza Khan intends to do next. He holds the office seven weeks and resigns on the seventh of January. The resignation is not a defeat. He will offer another as prime minister in July 1952 and be back in the job within five days with more power than he surrendered. The tactic is thirty-one years old by then, first used in a ministry he held for seven weeks.
suggested_refs: The cabinets of Ahmad Qavam, 1921-1922, and the ministerial instability between the 1921 coup and Reza Khan's rise

stops.name: Tabriz, Vali of Azerbaijan
stops.date_confidence: attested to 17 February to 12 July 1922; Tabriz is inferred as his seat from the province governed, and no specific government building is attested
stops.campa: In February he is sent north to govern Azerbaijan as Vali, a border province still raw from the Constitutionalist wars and from the rising of Sheikh Mohammad Khiabani, crushed two years before. He is out again by July. The capital keeps recalling him and keeps moving him on: five months here, seven weeks at Finance, a year in Fars. Successive governments want him in office and cannot leave him there. The premiership of 1951 is the first post he holds long enough to have to be removed from by force.
suggested_refs: The Khiabani rising in Tabriz, 1920, and its suppression

stops.name: Baharestan, the Foreign Ministry and the chamber
stops.date_confidence: attested to 30 May to 23 September 1923; the coordinates correct a wrong pair, 35.6841 / 51.426, that the first research pass reused across six entries
stops.campa: He becomes Foreign Minister under Mostowfi ol-Mamalek and is returned to the Majlis in June. The chamber at Baharestan, seat of parliament since the Constitutional Revolution, is the room in which he will cast every vote that defines him: against a dynasty in 1925, for nationalization in 1951, for emergency powers in 1952. He learns the room from the government benches first, as a minister answering questions rather than putting them. He will spend most of the next twenty-eight years shut out of it, and returns twice: to the fourteenth Majlis in 1944 and the seventeenth in 1952.
suggested_refs: The Baharestan chamber of the Majlis, Tehran, seat of parliament since 1906

stops.name: Baharestan, the vote against Reza Khan
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the opposition and the withdrawal from politics are attested, but the October dating and the content of the speech come from the secondary literature and were not read off a Majlis record in this pass
stops.campa: The bill transferring the throne from the Qajars to Reza Khan comes to the chamber and he speaks against it. His objection is constitutional and it is narrow: a man who is already prime minister and commander of the army cannot also be made sovereign without emptying the constitution of 1906 of its contents. He is one of a handful voting no. The bill passes. Reza Shah rules sixteen years, and for most of them Mosaddegh is a private citizen on his own land.
stops.quote: ...one man is to be king, Prime Minister and magistrate!
stops.quote_source: Mosaddegh objecting to the establishment of the Pahlavi dynasty, as quoted on mohammadmossadegh.com, which dates the line 1923 while the succession vote is of 1925; the discrepancy is unresolved
suggested_refs: The Majlis bill of 1925 deposing the Qajars and vesting the crown in Reza Khan
sources: Ervand Abrahamian, Iran Between Two Revolutions

stops.name: Ahmadabad, the years of the farm
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the withdrawal is well established in the biographical literature, the specific years are not, and the anchor date is a midpoint
stops.campa: Out of parliament and out of favor, he withdraws to Ahmadabad and farms it. Reza Shah's police imprison and kill other constitutionalists of his generation, and he tells associates he expects arrest at any hour. The arrest never comes. He spends the reign on the estate he was born on, waiting out a monarchy he voted against at its founding, and the wait runs sixteen years. The withdrawal preserves him. In 1941 he is the constitutionalist of 1925 who is still alive and still out of prison.
suggested_refs: The Ahmadabad estate under Reza Shah, 1925-1941
sources: Ervand Abrahamian, Iran Between Two Revolutions
Stephen Kinzer, All the Shah's Men

stops.name: Tehran, the abdication that reopens the country
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: British and Soviet armies occupy Iran and force Reza Shah off the throne. His son Mohammad Reza Pahlavi is installed at twenty-one, dependent on the powers that put him there. Press controls loosen, parties reappear, and the men the old shah silenced come back into public life. The son will outlast Mosaddegh by twelve years, kept on the throne in 1953 by an operation run out of a Tehran station of the CIA. Thirty-seven years after this abdication a revolution takes that throne away from him.
suggested_refs: The Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran, August-September 1941, and the abdication of Reza Shah

stops.name: Baharestan, return to the fourteenth Majlis
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1944; the month of the election is not fixed in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Tehran elects him to the fourteenth Majlis and he walks back into the chamber he denounced a dynasty from nineteen years earlier. He is sixty-one. The question waiting in the room is oil: the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company holds a concession over Iranian petroleum on terms no Iranian parliament wrote. In 1947 an electoral reform bill he champions fails and he announces his retirement from politics. The retirement lasts two years, and the second act of his life takes up the whole rest of it.
suggested_refs: The fourteenth Majlis, 1944-1946, and the oil concession question

stops.name: The Marble Palace, four days of bast
stops.date_confidence: attested to 15 October 1949; the coordinates correct a first-pass pin about 1.5 km off, and the outcome is stated as the source states it, a promise of fair elections rather than the partial recount the first pass claimed
stops.campa: A parliamentary election is rigged and he answers it with an old right rather than a new one. He leads a procession from his house on Kakh Street into the grounds of the Marble Palace and takes bast, the sanctuary a subject may claim on royal or sacred ground and hold until he is heard. Nineteen others sit down with him. They stay four days. The Shah gives in and promises fair and honest elections. The men who sat on that lawn will constitute a party three weeks later.
suggested_refs: The Marble Palace (Kakh-e Marmar), Imam Khomeini Street at Valiasr Street, Tehran

stops.name: Kakh Street, the National Front is founded
stops.date_confidence: attested to 12 November 1949, correcting a first pass that dated the founding to October and merged it with the bast; the street coordinates are approximate and the precise historic address is unverified
stops.campa: At his own house on the twelfth of November he and the men of the bast constitute the Jebhe-ye Melli, the National Front: nationalists, clerics, lawyers, and secular reformers who agree on very little except that the terms on which the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company holds Iranian petroleum are intolerable. The house becomes the coalition's working headquarters. Four years later a colonel of the Imperial Guard arrives at this door after midnight with a decree, and three days after that the house is shelled.
suggested_refs: The Mosaddegh residence on Kakh Street, Tehran, headquarters of the National Front
sources: Stephen Kinzer, All the Shah's Men

stops.name: Baharestan, the oil is nationalized
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Majlis votes to nationalize the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company and cancel its concession over Iranian petroleum. Mosaddegh, chairing the oil committee, has argued for years that the concession is both illegal and immoral. He is not yet prime minister when the vote carries. The company is Britain's largest overseas asset and the Abadan refinery is the largest in the world. Within six weeks the chamber will hand the man who argued for the vote the work of enforcing it.
stops.quote: The moral aspect of oil nationalization is more important than its economic aspect.
stops.quote_source: Attributed public statement on oil nationalization, reproduced on en.wikiquote.org and mohammadmossadegh.com; no primary transcript or date was located
suggested_refs: The Majlis nationalization law of March 1951 and the cancelled AIOC concession

stops.name: Tehran, confirmed prime minister
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; whether the confirmation was ceremonially at the palace or in the chamber is not specified in any source consulted
stops.campa: The Majlis votes confidence in him seventy-nine to twelve and the Shah confirms him as prime minister. He is sixty-eight. He takes the office on the condition that the nationalization law be carried out, which means dispossessing a British corporation of the industry that fuels the Royal Navy. He will hold the premiership two years and four months, with one interruption of five days, and will leave it under artillery fire from his own army. The chamber that raises him is the last Iranian parliament for a quarter of a century that anyone treats as a source of power.
suggested_refs: The Majlis confidence vote of 28 April 1951, 79 to 12

stops.name: Abadan, the refinery changes hands
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1951 for the takeover; no evidence was found that Mosaddegh ever travelled to Abadan, and this pin marks the event and not a footfall, since he directed the nationalization from Tehran
stops.campa: Iranian officials take physical possession of the Abadan refinery, then the largest in the world. British technicians withdraw over the following months, Britain organizes a boycott of Iranian oil and blockades its export, and the plant's output collapses. The country loses the revenue that nationalization was supposed to deliver and keeps the ownership it fought for. There is no attested record of Mosaddegh setting foot in Abadan during the crisis. He runs the entire confrontation from Tehran.
stops.quote: Our long years of negotiations with foreign countries... have yielded no results thus far. With the oil revenues, we could meet our entire budget and combat poverty, disease, and backwardness among our people.
stops.quote_source: Speech of 21 June 1951, quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Mohammad Mosaddegh' citing M. Fateh, Panjah Sal-e Naft-e Iran (Fifty Years of Iranian Oil), p. 525; the internal ellipsis is in the sourced text and is restored here
suggested_refs: The Abadan refinery, Khuzestan, and the British boycott of Iranian oil, 1951-1953
sources: M. Fateh, Panjah Sal-e Naft-e Iran, p. 525

stops.name: Cairo, the stop at al-Azhar
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the Cairo stopover is a traditionally cited detail of the 1951 trip, cited across secondary accounts but not fixed to a verified itinerary, and the leg it belongs to is unknown
stops.campa: On one leg of the journey between Tehran and New York he stops in Cairo, and tradition places him at al-Azhar and in the company of Egyptian officials. Egypt is that year in its own quarrel with Britain over the Suez Canal Zone. The anti-colonial nationalism of the Arab world takes him for its own, and Nasser will later name a Cairo street after him. The street outlasts his government by decades. The itinerary of the stop is not fixed in any source consulted.
suggested_refs: Al-Azhar Mosque, Cairo, and the 1951 Egyptian abrogation of the Anglo-Egyptian treaty

stops.name: Lake Success, before the Security Council
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the venue is given as Lake Success, the Council's temporary Long Island headquarters in 1951 before the 1952 move to Manhattan, and the exact meeting site was not re-verified
stops.campa: Britain brings its complaint to the Security Council and Iran's prime minister answers it in person, which heads of government do not do. He speaks in Persian through an interpreter and argues that a state which owns a resource may take back the industry built on top of it. The Council defers the matter pending the International Court of Justice. He has moved the quarrel out of the Foreign Office and into a room where Iran is a member state and Britain is one vote among eleven.
stops.quote: ...the petroleum industry has contributed nothing to well-being of the people or to the technological progress or industrial development of my country.
stops.quote_source: Address to the UN Security Council, 15 October 1951, verbatim record S/PV.560, as quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Mohammad Mosaddegh'; the record itself is live at docs.un.org but its body text could not be retrieved in this pass, and the wording, which lacks a definite article, is given as the source gives it
suggested_refs: UN Security Council verbatim record S/PV.560, 560th meeting, 15 October 1951
sources: UN document S/PV.560 (existence confirmed, text not retrieved)

stops.name: The White House, Truman and Acheson
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the meetings are well documented in the secondary literature but were not re-verified against primary record, and the exact day is approximate
stops.campa: From New York he goes to Washington and meets President Truman and Secretary of State Acheson. The Americans are sympathetic to Iranian sovereignty, impatient with British imperial nostalgia, and unwilling to do anything at all about the boycott. Truman will not join a covert operation against him. American reporters describe an old man steadied and carried through his own appearances, weeping and near collapse; sources divide on the venue and on whether the frailty was staged. The sympathy expires with the administration.
suggested_refs: The Truman administration's refusal to join the British operation against Mosaddegh, 1951-1952
sources: Stephen Kinzer, All the Shah's Men
Mark Gasiorowski and Malcolm Byrne, Mohammad Mosaddeq and the 1953 Coup in Iran

stops.name: Mehrabad, the return to the crowds
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the scale of the welcome is generally reported, but the airport arrival itself was not independently verified and the day is approximate
stops.campa: He comes home from America and Europe to one of the largest crowds Tehran has ever put into the street. He has stood in front of the Security Council and the government of the United States and conceded nothing, and the country reads it exactly that way. This is the summit of his popularity. Everything after is a descent conducted under a boycott that empties the treasury, and the crowd that meets him at Mehrabad is the same instrument that will be bought against him with American money in August 1953.
suggested_refs: Mehrabad Airport, Tehran, and the November 1951 reception
sources: Stephen Kinzer, All the Shah's Men

stops.name: Tehran, the Land Reform Act
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1952 only; no month is given in the sources consulted and the anchor defaults to January
stops.campa: His government passes a Land Reform Act requiring landlords to put twenty percent of their revenues toward rural development and the welfare of the men who work the land. It is a modest law and it makes him a permanent enemy of the landholding class, whose deputies sit in his parliament and whose districts return them. The oil quarrel is with Britain. This one is domestic, and the coalition that eventually stands aside for the coup is assembled in part out of it.
suggested_refs: The Iranian Land Reform Act of 1952 and the twenty percent revenue allocation

stops.name: Baharestan, the voting halted at quorum
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1952; the specific month of the halt is not fixed in the sources consulted, and the reason is corrected here from the first pass, which had the geography of his support exactly backwards
stops.campa: The elections to the seventeenth Majlis go his way in the cities. National Front candidates take all twelve Tehran seats on doubled turnout. In the rural districts, where landlords control the vote, they do not. He stops the voting once seventy-nine of one hundred and thirty-six deputies have been returned, a bare quorum, so that the countryside cannot seat a majority against him. He has defended the constitution since 1925 by insisting that elections be honest. He now halts one because he is losing it.
suggested_refs: The 1952 Iranian legislative election and the seventeenth Majlis, seated at 79 of 136

stops.name: The Peace Palace, before the International Court
stops.date_confidence: attested to the public sittings of 9-23 June 1952, correcting a first pass that dated this appearance to June 1951 and thereby placed it before the October 1951 UN trip rather than after it
stops.campa: He travels to The Hague and argues in person that the International Court has no jurisdiction over what is a contract between a state and a company rather than a treaty between two states. The sittings run through June and resume in July. On the twenty-second of July the Court agrees that it lacks jurisdiction, and Iran wins. By the time the judgment is read he has resigned, been replaced, and been returned to office by a rising in the streets of Tehran, all inside the same week.
stops.quote: There is no political or moral yardstick by which the court can measure its judgment in the case of nationalization of the oil industry in Iran.
stops.quote_source: Statement refusing International Court of Justice jurisdiction over the nationalization dispute, as quoted on en.wikiquote.org; the underlying ICJ pleadings were not retrieved in this pass
suggested_refs: ICJ case record, Anglo-Iranian Oil Co. (United Kingdom v. Iran), icj-cij.org/case/16, judgment of 22 July 1952
sources: ICJ case record, Anglo-Iranian Oil Co. (UK v. Iran)
Mostafa Elm, Oil, Power, and Principle

stops.name: Tehran, the resignation over the War Ministry
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He asks the Shah for the Ministry of War, which means control of the officer corps and of every appointment inside it. The Shah refuses. Mosaddegh resigns on the sixteenth of July, and Ahmad Qavam, the man who made him finance minister thirty-one years earlier, is appointed in his place. The army is the one instrument of the state he has never held. Thirteen months later the officer corps he was refused delivers his government to the Central Intelligence Agency.
stops.quote: In the present situation, the struggle started by the Iranian people cannot be brought to a victorious conclusion.
stops.quote_source: Resignation statement, 16 July 1952, as quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Mohammad Mosaddegh'
suggested_refs: The July 1952 dispute over the Ministry of War and military appointments

stops.name: Baharestan Square, the Thirtieth of Tir
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the reappointment with the War Ministry falls on the same date as the uprising
stops.campa: Qavam's appointment puts Tehran in the street. The National Front, the bazaar, and the Tudeh Party call a general strike; crowds fill Baharestan Square and the avenues around it; the army fires and dozens are killed. On the thirtieth of Tir the military withdraws from the streets, Qavam falls after five days in office, and Mosaddegh is reappointed with the War Ministry he was refused. The uprising hands him the army. It also spends the popular credit he will need in August of the following year.
suggested_refs: The Si-ye Tir uprising, 21 July 1952, and its dead
sources: Ervand Abrahamian, Iran Between Two Revolutions
Homa Katouzian, on the July 1952 crisis

stops.name: London, Churchill turns to a new administration
stops.date_confidence: attested to early 1953; the specific date of Churchill's decision is not fixed, and the anchor defaults to January, when the Eisenhower administration took office
stops.campa: Churchill's government has wanted Mosaddegh removed since the nationalization and has been refused by Truman, who will not put the United States behind a British concession. In January the Eisenhower administration takes office. Churchill solicits it, arguing that Iran is drifting toward the Tudeh Party and the Soviet Union, and Washington agrees. The operation is British in origin and American in execution. Three weeks before Nassiri knocks, Fidel Castro attacks the Moncada Barracks in Cuba.
suggested_refs: The Truman administration's refusal and the Eisenhower administration's assent to TPAJAX, 1952-1953

stops.name: Tehran, the exchange seized and the ministers taken
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the night of the fifteenth, Colonel Nematollah Nassiri's Imperial Guard units move to arrest the members of the government. The army takes Tehran's central telephone exchange, which is how a capital is cut in two. Foreign Minister Hossein Fatemi, who has attacked the Shah in print more sharply than anyone else in the cabinet, is seized along with other officials. Fatemi is released within days, rearrested once the coup succeeds, and shot by firing squad the following year.
suggested_refs: Hossein Fatemi, foreign minister, executed by firing squad in 1954

stops.name: Kakh Street, Nassiri at the door with a firman
stops.date_confidence: attested to the early hours of 16 August; the street coordinates are approximate
stops.campa: Colonel Nassiri arrives at the prime minister's house after midnight carrying the Shah's decree of dismissal. Mosaddegh has been warned. He examines the firman, questions whether it is authentic, and has the colonel arrested on his own doorstep. The first attempt of Operation Ajax collapses within the hour. Loyal troops hold the city by morning and the government announces that a coup has been defeated, which is true, and that the danger has passed, which is not.
suggested_refs: The royal firman of dismissal served on Mosaddegh, 16 August 1953

stops.name: Ramsar, the Shah leaves the country
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Shah was not in Tehran but at his villa at Kelardasht, was informed at about four in the morning that Nassiri's mission had failed, and flew by small plane to Ramsar before Baghdad and then Rome, correcting a first pass that placed him in Tehran and flew him straight to Baghdad
stops.campa: The Shah is not in Tehran. He is at his villa at Kelardasht on the Caspian coast, and at about four in the morning he learns that the colonel has been arrested and the decree refused. He takes a small plane to Ramsar, flies on to Baghdad, and is flown from there to Rome. He has signed a decree dismissing his prime minister and left his own country within twelve hours of its being served. He is back in Tehran inside a week, restored by other men's hands.
suggested_refs: The Shah's flight of 16 August 1953: Kelardasht, Ramsar, Baghdad, Rome

stops.name: Kakh Street, the house shelled
stops.date_confidence: attested for the overthrow and the shelling; the pajama detail is a widely repeated tradition and is not independently confirmed in any source consulted
stops.campa: General Fazlollah Zahedi has been hidden in a CIA safehouse, and the crowds now moving through Tehran are organized and paid for by the station Kermit Roosevelt Jr. runs in coordination with Britain's MI6. On the nineteenth they converge on the prime minister's house with army units, tanks, and artillery. The house is shelled and looted. Mosaddegh goes over the garden wall into a neighboring property, in his pajamas by an account repeated everywhere and confirmed nowhere. Between two and three hundred die in the unrest.
suggested_refs: TPAJAX, the CIA-paid crowds of 19 August 1953, and the installation of Fazlollah Zahedi
sources: Stephen Kinzer, All the Shah's Men

stops.name: Tehran, the surrender the next morning
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the surrender on 20 August is attested and corrects a first pass that had him arrested on the 19th, but the address of the neighboring house was not independently verified
stops.campa: He hides one night. In the morning, with Zahedi installed as prime minister and the Shah on his way back from Rome, he walks out and gives himself up rather than run for a border. Twenty-eight months after the confidence vote of seventy-nine to twelve, the government is over, and the man who took Britain to the Security Council and the International Court is in a military cell. In Chile twenty years later the same method removes Salvador Allende and installs Augusto Pinochet. The men who ran the Tehran operation expected it to fail.
suggested_refs: The surrender of 20 August 1953 and the transfer to military custody
sources: Stephen Kinzer, All the Shah's Men
Mark Gasiorowski and Malcolm Byrne, Mohammad Mosaddeq and the 1953 Coup in Iran

stops.name: Tehran, the military tribunal
stops.date_confidence: attested to November and December 1953 for the proceedings and to 19 December for the defence statement; the Officers' Club as the venue is a common identification in the coup literature and its coordinates are an estimate
stops.campa: He is tried by a military tribunal on charges amounting to treason against the Shah. He conducts much of his own defence, at length, in front of broadcast microphones, and turns the proceeding into the last public platform he will be given. He does not deny the nationalization. He argues that it was lawful, that the government removed on the nineteenth of August was the legal government of Iran, and that the court trying him owes its existence to the men who removed it.
stops.quote: Yes, my sin, my greater sin, and even my greatest sin is that I nationalized Iran's oil industry and discarded the system of political and economic exploitation by the world's greatest empire.
stops.quote_source: Defence statement before the military tribunal, 19 December 1953, as reproduced on mohammadmossadegh.com and en.wikiquote.org; the original Persian court record was not located in this pass
suggested_refs: The military tribunal of November-December 1953 and Mosaddegh's own defence
sources: Mark Gasiorowski and Malcolm Byrne, Mohammad Mosaddeq and the 1953 Coup in Iran
Stephen Kinzer, All the Shah's Men

stops.name: Tehran, three years in solitary
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the sentence of 21 December 1953 and the three-year term are attested, but the prison building and its coordinates are an estimate and the first pass tagged this as attested while conceding in its own note that the location was a guess
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of December he is sentenced to three years of solitary confinement. The prosecution asked for death and did not get it. He serves the term in a military prison in Tehran. Outside it, the National Front is broken at the polls in 1954, an international consortium takes over the oil that was nationalized, and the Shah begins the twenty-five years of personal rule the coup bought him, the Iran in which Giuseppe Tucci will run Italian archaeological missions from 1959 to 1978.
suggested_refs: The 1954 consortium agreement replacing the nationalized AIOC

stops.name: Ahmadabad, house arrest on his own land
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1956 for the beginning of the confinement; the month is not fixed in the sources consulted and the anchor is approximate
stops.campa: He comes out of prison into a confinement with no end date. He is sent to Ahmadabad, the estate he was born on and farmed through Reza Shah's reign, and forbidden to leave it, to receive visitors freely, or to speak in public. The state that watches him is the state he governed. He spends eleven years there writing memoirs that circulate only after his death, on the same ground where he waited out the father, now under the son. The first confinement on this land was his own choice. This one is not.
suggested_refs: Khaterat va Ta'allomat-e Mosaddegh (Memoirs and Sufferings of Mosaddegh), written under house arrest

stops.name: Najmieh Hospital, Tehran, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the hospital coordinates are an estimate, and this corrects the project's own afterlife lens, which had him dying at Ahmadabad rather than being brought into Tehran for treatment
stops.campa: In his final illness he is brought from Ahmadabad into Tehran and dies at Najmieh Hospital on the fifth of March, eighty-four years old. He has been out of office for fourteen years and confined for thirteen of them. The government is left with the only question about him that remains: where a man this popular may be put into the ground, and whether anyone may be permitted to stand there. Every element of the funeral becomes a decision about public order, taken by the men who took the state from him.
suggested_refs: Najmieh Hospital, Tehran, where Mosaddegh died on 5 March 1967

stops.name: Ibn Babuyeh cemetery, the burial he asked for and did not get
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the refusal is reported in the Persian Wikipedia article but the date of the decision is not fixed, and the anchor is the day after his death
stops.campa: He had asked to be buried at Ibn Babuyeh in Rey, among the dead of the Thirtieth of Tir, the crowd that put him back into office in July 1952. The government refuses. A grave in a public cemetery beside those martyrs would be a place people could go to, and a place people can go to becomes a demonstration. The dead of 1952 stay where they are and he is not brought to them. The wish survives only in the accounts of those who heard him make it, which is why it is recorded here as tradition rather than as record.
suggested_refs: Ibn Babuyeh cemetery, Rey, burial ground of the 30 Tir 1952 dead

stops.name: Ahmadabad, buried beneath the dining room
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the burial inside the house is attested and the source is specific that it is under the dining room, but the exact date of interment is not given
stops.campa: He is buried inside his own house at Ahmadabad, under the floor of the dining room, with no state funeral. The estate is where he was born in 1882, where he farmed out Reza Shah's reign, where the son's government kept him eleven years, and now where he lies. The Pahlavi state has arranged that the most popular man in modern Iranian politics has no grave the public can reach. The compound falls into serious disrepair under the restrictions imposed on the site.
suggested_refs: The grave under the dining-room floor at Ahmadabad-e Mosaddeq

stops.name: Ahmadabad, the school named and unnamed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1979 for the naming; the date of the later renaming is not given in the source
stops.campa: In the revolution the villagers of Ahmadabad vote to name their high school after the man buried in the house. Ayatollah Khomeini denounces Mosaddegh, and the school is renamed Emam Khomeini High School. The revolution that ends the monarchy the coup preserved does not adopt him. It takes up the grievance and puts down the man: a Qajar aristocrat and constitutional lawyer who carried his case to the Security Council and the International Court and lost the country regardless.
suggested_refs: The high school at Ahmadabad-e Mosaddeq, named by popular vote in 1979 and later renamed

stops.name: Tehran, the throne the coup saved is taken
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Twenty-six years after Operation Ajax restored him to full power, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi leaves Iran for the last time and the monarchy ends. Michel Foucault has walked these demonstrations for Corriere della Sera through the autumn and gone to Qom to sit with clerics explaining a government founded on religion; Khomeini has directed the whole thing from a garden at Neauphle-le-Chateau outside Paris. Every actor of 1979 is standing on ground the coup of 1953 prepared.
suggested_refs: Foucault's Iranian dispatches for Corriere della Sera, autumn 1978

stops.name: Washington, the acknowledgment
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2013; the release was timed to the sixtieth anniversary of the coup and the day is given accordingly
stops.campa: Sixty years after the nineteenth of August, the United States government formally acknowledges the CIA's role in the coup, in documents declassified under the Obama administration. Every Iranian government since 1953 has said it. The denial outlived Mosaddegh by forty-six years and Kermit Roosevelt Jr. by a great many interviews. The declassified documents settle no argument about policy. They record that the operation happened and that the agency ran it.
suggested_refs: The 2013 declassification acknowledging CIA authorship of the 1953 coup

stops.name: Telluride, the film that finds Darbyshire
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Coup 53, directed by Taghi Amirani and cut and co-written by Walter Murch, premieres at Telluride. It is built around a rediscovered interview transcript in which the MI6 officer Norman Darbyshire states that he plotted Operation Ajax jointly with the CIA. Ralph Fiennes reads the recovered passages on screen. The film also uses archival footage from End of Empire, the 1985 Granada Television series in which Darbyshire's own testimony had been left out of the broadcast.
suggested_refs: The Darbyshire transcript recovered for Coup 53 (2019)
End of Empire, Granada Television, 1985

stops.name: Ahmadabad, the house and the name
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the disrepair of the compound is described in the source as a current condition without any date, and the anchor is a placeholder for the present
stops.campa: The village is now called Ahmadabad-e Mosaddeq. A Dr. Mosaddegh street exists in Tehran, and another in Cairo, named by Nasser for a fellow enemy of empire. Mosaddeghism is catalogued as a current of Iranian liberalism and social democracy with no party and no state behind it. The house he is buried in stands in serious disrepair under restrictions on the site. The atlas already holds Cyrus at Pasargadae and Zoroaster in Media: the same plateau, and a twentieth-century argument about who owns what lies under it.
suggested_refs: Mosaddeghism as a current in Iranian political thought
